title: Greedy Best-First in Žižkov: Fast or Tricky?
description: Watch Greedy Best-First race across a street-graph of Žižkov, always chasing the goal with the most promising heuristic. It’s quick, but sometimes it can get trapped by locally “best-looking” turns—perfect for learning how heuristic search behaves on real maps.
ig_caption:
🧭✨ **Greedy Best-First** doesn’t “think ahead”—it *chooses what looks closest to the target right now*.

On a real street map turned into a **graph** (nodes = intersections, edges = road segments with weights/constraints), the algorithm ranks frontier nodes by a heuristic **h(n)** (e.g., straight-line distance to the destination). At each step, it expands the node with the smallest **h(n)**, making it a classic **informed graph search** strategy.

⚠️ The tradeoff: because it doesn’t primarily minimize total path cost **g(n)**, it can yield **non-optimal routes**—especially in neighborhoods with “detours that look shorter” by distance alone (hello, complex intersection geometry!).

🎥 In this visualization, watch how the frontier explores and how heuristic bias shapes the route.

yt_description:
Prague Žižkov pathfinding visualization using **Greedy Best-First** (heuristic search)! 🚦

In this YouTube Shorts clip, we convert real street maps into a **graph** and run **Greedy Best-First**: at each step, the algorithm expands the frontier node with the smallest heuristic distance to the goal.

You’ll see how heuristic bias can make routes fast but not always optimal—perfect for learning **graph search**, **informed algorithms**, and **AI navigation**.
